families.title: Complete a square and recover its vertex
families.learner_decisions: Scale the completed square correctly and distinguish the extreme ordinate from its attaining abscissa.
families.givens_and_unknowns: Given quadratic coefficients or one coefficient fixed by a point; unknown completed form and vertex.
families.constraints: Nonzero leading coefficient; its sign determines maximum/minimum. Preserve fractional shifts exactly.
families.representation_and_response: Algebraic input; completed expression and point/value output. A full graph is a separate linked demand.
families.scaffolding_and_connected_parts: Completion may precede an explicitly hence vertex; retain that chain rather than demand a new derivation.
families.alternative_methods: Completion directly; vertex formula checks coordinates but does not replace expressly requested completed form.
families.units_and_precision: Exact symbolic values unless a member explicitly asks rounding. Each member retains its original precision and answer records; no examination-wide rule is inferred from a key display.
families.answer_form: Equivalent completed-square expression and requested ordered pair or extreme value/attaining x.
families.difficulty_progression: YM Example22 andTry22 introduce nonunit leading coefficients and fractional shifts;Exercise9 adds point-constrained preparation.
families.distinction_basis: Different from solving zeros, constructing a graph or recovering unknown coefficients from graph data.

families.title: Solve an original radical equation with domain filtering
families.learner_decisions: Isolate roots with their sign restrictions, square only when justified and test all candidates in the original equation.
families.givens_and_unknowns: One or two principal square roots, sometimes reciprocal; unknown real solution set.
families.constraints: Original radicands nonnegative; isolated RHS nonnegative; reciprocal root strictly positive. Empty/singleton/two-root sets are intentional branches.
families.representation_and_response: Equation to exact verified roots and rejection reasoning.
families.scaffolding_and_connected_parts: The method may need two squarings; source no-solution cases must remain valid cases rather than generator failures.
families.alternative_methods: Domain/sign bounds may disprove solvability before squaring; suitable substitutions are alternatives where the source structure allows.
families.units_and_precision: Exact symbolic values unless a member explicitly asks rounding. Each member retains its original precision and answer records; no examination-wide rule is inferred from a key display.
families.answer_form: Complete original-root set, including an explicit empty set where warranted.
families.difficulty_progression: YM Example10 has an extraneous squared candidate;Example11 has two valid roots after two squarings;Try10Q2 includes an impossible domain case.
families.distinction_basis: This is the recovery/filtering branch rather than an assumption that every radical equation first needs recognition of a quadratic substitution.

insights.title: Completed form, vertex and quadratic sketch
insights.teaching_comparison: YM separates prescribed completion, identifying the extreme value and its abscissa, and drawing a consistent sketch. Example22 changes the outer coefficient;Example23 changes the orientation. It then reverses the direction in graph-to-equation examples. Goldie2&3 largely assumes this Mathematics1background:Exercise1B23 asks the greatest value of a quadratic obtained by subtracting two cubics, but does not supply a parallel standalone quadratic-sketch sequence. GoldieC6Prompt1 merely permits algebraic solution methods; choosing completion in an author solution is not evidence that the source assesses completion.
insights.examination_comparison: NSSCAS2022P1Q1(a)(b) explicitly pairs prescribed completed form with a turning point. The full-sketch textbook chains add response evidence beyond those two exam parts. Goldie’s composite maximum task combines theorem constraints and quadratic interpretation, so its entire question is not the same type as a short completed-form part. Official convention079 requires visible quadratic solving where applicable; it is not a ban on valid alternate vertex calculations when the question allows them.
insights.difficulty_and_grade_bounds: GradeE01 explicitly includes completion, turning point and sketch;GradeC01 emphasises interpretation of completed form. YM develops from monic forms to scaled/fractional vertices and linked sketches. Goldie1B23 is harder through preceding coefficient recovery, not through larger numbers. GradeA01’s coupled algebra provides contextual upper-demand evidence, not a numeric parameter domain or a grade assigned to each textbook item.
insights.pitfalls: YM Try21Q1 has a correct coordinate with a wrong guide label; this is a source defect, not learner-error prevalence. Proposed feedback should distinguish wrong outer scaling, confusing the minimum ordinate with the attaining x, and a graph contradicting otherwise correct coordinates. No examiner-specific frequency is claimed for those three distinctions.
insights.gaps_and_representations: YM has explicit sketch practice;the inspected Goldie census has no directly assessed standalone quadratic-sketch item. The exam completion/vertex chain is therefore supported mainly by YM. A graph supplied for reconstruction is different evidence from a graph produced as an answer.
insights.implications_for_step3: Propose preserving completion→vertex→sketch as a connected scaffold and keeping optional formula checks distinct from a prescribed completed expression. Generate all eventual graph labels from the same polynomial. Do not turn the four solving methods shown for one YM example into four recipes.

insights.title: Discriminants, parameter conditions and universal root proofs
insights.teaching_comparison: YM gives sign/root-count tables before fixed-equation classification, parameter ranges, and universal proofs. Example15 has one parameter condition;Try16Q3 makes the leading coefficient vanish at a candidate parameter. Example19’s real-parameter rationality claim is false;Try19 supplies integer restrictions that change what can be proved. Goldie uses quadratic factors inside polynomial work but has no corresponding directly assessed discriminant/parameter sequence in the inspected inventory; that incidental method must not be promoted to an extra direct demand.
insights.examination_comparison: NSSCAS2022P1Q4 asks a parameter set for unequal real roots;2021P1Q10(b) asks a universal real-root argument;2025P1Q1(a) asks rationality for a nonzero integer parameter. They need different conclusions. Convention095 requires the discriminant positivity argument in its2021proof context. Convention102 asks the2022connected interval to be written as a double inequality; that question-specific remark is not a universal ban on mathematically equivalent set notation.
insights.difficulty_and_grade_bounds: GradeE01 covers computing a discriminant, whileC01 adds interpretation of real roots. A01 supports more coupled algebra and coefficient-domain reasoning, but does not state a numerical ceiling for parameter coefficients. YM’s hard boundary is logical:linear degeneration, a zero discriminant, or rational versus merely real coefficients. Do not classify difficulty by coefficient magnitude alone.
insights.pitfalls: A square is nonnegative, not always positive. YM’s source commentary and several proofs omit zero or linear cases; these are registered source shortcomings. ERR01 corroborates the need for complete proof and a conclusion, but does not establish how often each textbook-specific mistake occurs among learners.
insights.gaps_and_representations: YM provides both routine fixed-equation drills and stronger universal proofs. A given-root coefficient-recovery drill is prerequisite algebra, not automatically the discriminant parameter-condition demand. Held NSSCAS2023P1Q1(b) is not a valid exemplar; its hold remains binding even though the syllabus demand has other sources.
insights.implications_for_step3: Propose separate decisions for fixed root classification, solving a parameter condition, and proving an all-parameter/rationality claim. Every eventual quadratic proof should test the leading coefficient before invoking a quadratic theorem. The analysis audit repaired12YMrecords missing the explicit parameter-condition demand; it did not infer coverage from these family labels.

insights.title: Identity meaning and coefficients in a specified form
insights.teaching_comparison: YM explicitly contrasts identities, conditional equations and inequalities in its teaching tables, then asks coefficients in prescribed square, product and rational forms. GoldieC7Prompt1 explicitly asks why an identity symbol changes to equality when a particular value is substituted; that retained prompt is within8227even though the surrounding unrestricted partial-fraction method is not. Goldie8E4/8H3 supply the rational decomposition template before coefficient determination and later integration. Given template and free choice of a decomposition are different scope decisions.
insights.examination_comparison: NSSCAS2023P1Q3 supplies a rational identity;2024P1Q2 supplies a quartic product identity. Both directly assess coefficient determination. Neither alone demonstrates that a learner can explain identity versus conditional equation. In the inspected papers there is no usable direct part for that separate distinction; Goldie’s explicit prompt supplies textbook-derived practice, while YM’s comparison tables provide teaching support.
insights.difficulty_and_grade_bounds: GradeC01 names the distinction and coefficient determination;A01 adds two or more coupled unknowns. Routine prescribed-square constants are easier than simultaneous product coefficients, correlated sign pairs or a template followed by an integral. The level descriptor does not justify requiring general partial fractions or complex roots.
insights.pitfalls: An identity must hold throughout its common domain; rational denominator exclusions remain after clearing denominators. A conditional equality is not a different mathematical species from every identity:the distinction is all admitted inputs versus a condition to solve. YM’s explanatory table needs that qualification. These are source/author reasoning notes; no examiner-specific identity misconception is asserted without a matching report excerpt.
insights.gaps_and_representations: The explicit identity-distinction task comes from an otherwise excluded chapter, showing why scope must be checked at facet level. Conversely, many coefficient exercises do not ask the conceptual distinction and must not erase that gap. Textbook integration chains extend the observed coefficient part rather than establish a new exam award pattern.
insights.implications_for_step3: Propose keeping the conceptual distinction inspectable apart from coefficient solving. Preserve supplied rational templates, original exclusions and correlated constant tuples. Treat extra integration as a connected branch when the source asks it; do not use these records to author unrestricted partial-fraction recipes.

insights.title: Quadratic transformations and original-variable recovery
insights.teaching_comparison: YM progresses from equations quadratic inx² to nonnegative square-root substitutions, reciprocal powers, positive exponentials and a nested rational expression. It separately teaches original radical equations where squaring creates candidates needing rejection. Goldie1B8 factors a quartic as a quadratic inx², but the source asks factorisation and zero count; the inventory does not claim that every intermediate recognition step is an independently assessed substitution demand.
insights.examination_comparison: NSSCAS2021P1Q3(a)(b) has an explicit HENCE chain from a quartic to a nested radical expression. ERR10 identifies failure to recover the original variable;ERR02 stresses retaining HENCE dependence. The textbook’s stand-alone radical problems practise filtering but do not by themselves cover the full exam recognition-and-reuse chain.
insights.difficulty_and_grade_bounds: GradeA01 explicitly names recognising and solving an equation quadratic in a function ofx. Ordinary prior quadratic solving is a scaffold, not a substitute for that demand. The harder textbook cases change the intermediate range or inversion multiplicity:even powers, odd real roots, reciprocal exclusion and a positive exponential are genuine structural differences. No grade-specific numerical parameter bounds are decided here.
insights.pitfalls: Negative square-root/exponential intermediate values must be rejected; odd-root negatives may be valid; reciprocals exclude zero. YM Example10’s extraneous squared candidate andTry13’s different inverse ranges provide concrete contrast. ERR10 supports the recovery issue broadly, not an inferred diagnosis from any one wrong final answer. Goldie1B8’s wrong first factorisation is a source defect; a later correct count does not validate the erroneous step.
insights.gaps_and_representations: The retained Goldie book provides factorisation context but not the full YM progression of directly assessed transformation/recovery tasks. Branch breadth therefore comes mainly from YM plus the examined HENCE chain. A reciprocal equation reduced by denominator clearing must keep its original forbidden values.
insights.implications_for_step3: Propose retaining the original equation and intermediate-domain ledger in future solutions. Keep a preceding ordinary equation as scaffold only when its result is actually reused. Verify every recovered candidate in the original; do not count expanded root sets or changed notation as new problem types.

insights.title: Recover quadratic and cubic equations from sufficient information
insights.teaching_comparison: YM separates root-factor reconstruction from vertex-led reconstruction, then introduces cubics with crossing/touching roots and an extra scaling point. Multiple curves share axes inExample27, requiring careful label/scale reading. Goldie1B7 reverses its usual supplied-polynomial sequence:a given cubic graph fixes multiplicities and scale before a new equation is solved. Goldie11B9(i) retains a real-root quadratic construction, while its later complex-root cases remain excluded.
insights.examination_comparison: NSSCAS2021P1Q2 supplies a parabola with roots and minimum, allowing root-factor or vertex form. There is no usable cubic-reconstruction part in the inspected NSSCAS2021–2025mapping. The cubic textbook examples support that prescribed demand without becoming Namibian examination evidence or proving examination frequency.
insights.difficulty_and_grade_bounds: GradeC01 says recover an equation from sufficient graph information;A01 explicitly mentions quadratic and cubic graphs. YM’s simple roots/intercept cases are less connected than rational touching factors, three simultaneous curves or mixed constraints requiring a coefficient system. GradeE01’s quadratic completion/sketch statement does not itself warrant cubic-reconstruction difficulty. These are qualitative source comparisons, not assigned item grades.
insights.pitfalls: A touching root carries multiplicity; its factor scaling must be compensated globally. The source’s categorical advice against a fractional linear factor is misleading:equivalent scaled factors are valid when the outer coefficient changes consistently. A scaling point that is already a zero does not determine the scale. These are mathematical/author cautions; no specific examiner-error frequency is claimed.
insights.gaps_and_representations: Both books supply cubic reconstruction although the local examined sample does not. A drawing supplied as data and a drawing required as a response are distinct. Graph-derived root data, a prose vertex and purely algebraic root information should retain their original representation labels.
insights.implications_for_step3: Propose parameterising redundant graph labels from one polynomial and checking all incidences. Keep vertex-led, root-led and multiplicity/mixed-data branches explicit. Preserve the textbook-only cubic demand as a visible syllabus gap with source support, not an invented exam-observed label.

insights.title: Critical values, intervals and boundary evidence
insights.teaching_comparison: YM develops an inequality from a quadratic graph or factorisation, explicitly contrasts upward/downward signs and often requests a number line. ItsTry29Q4 first supplies an equation-solving scaffold with2dp endpoints. Goldie’s retained algebra chapter concentrates on modulus inequalities rather than a parallel standalone quadratic-inequality sequence; their squared comparisons can use quadratic sign analysis as a component, but that does not automatically count as direct quadratic-interval coverage.
insights.examination_comparison: NSSCAS2023P1Q1(a) compares a quadratic ordinate with a horizontal level;2025P1Q1(b) uses a parameter value fixed by the preceding part. Both require a complete solution set. Explicit number-line drawings are additional textbook evidence; roots alone cannot replace the inequality answer. Convention102 is a specific reminder about connected interval expression in the2022parameter question, not a universal representation policy.
insights.difficulty_and_grade_bounds: GradeC01 explicitly includes solving quadratic inequalities. YM’s harder cases add collection across both sides, negative outer coefficients, rounded displayed roots and connected equality-first structure. A01/A11provide related compound algebra and modulus contexts, but do not assign a grade solely from two intervals rather than one. E01 supplies supporting quadratic skills without expressly naming the whole interval demand.
insights.pitfalls: Endpoint inclusion follows the original strict/nonstrict relation. YM Try29Q1(b)’s filled dots conflict with its strict textual key;Try29Q3has a wrong supplementary boundary label. These are source defects. A generic wrong-root diagnosis would miss a correct boundary with an incorrect open/closed endpoint; no examiner-specific prevalence is claimed.
insights.gaps_and_representations: The inspected inventory has direct quadratic-inequality practice inYM, whileGoldie’s modulus questions supply related components. Exam comparisons should preserve the difference. The line/curve parameter branch additionally needs a geometric interpretation and can include linear degeneration.
insights.implications_for_step3: Propose keeping exact critical values internally and applying requested rounding only at display. Validate symbolic intervals against number-line endpoints and an interior/exterior test point. Keep a HENCE equality scaffold when its roots are meant to be reused.
